guides.title: Jenné-jeno and the Inland Niger Delta
guides.description: Excavated flood-plain mounds revealing sub-Saharan Africa’s earliest indigenous clustered urbanism from 250 BCE through historic Jenné.
guides.intro: For generations historians assumed that cities south of the Sahara emerged only after Arab merchants reached the Niger Bend. Excavations beginning at Jenné-jeno in 1977 overturned that picture, uncovering an entire urban civilization thriving on the Inland Niger Delta floodplain a thousand years earlier.
guides.scope: Archaeological sequences across Jenné-jeno, Dia Shoma, Sadia, Bandiagara/Ounjougou, and historical Jenné from Early Holocene wetlands through c. 1900 CE.

map.scope: Modern Inland Niger Delta and Bandiagara plateau locality anchors. River channels shift seasonally; points mark archaeological research areas, not ancient city limits.

points.label: Jenné-jeno
points.description: Main 33-hectare flood-plain mound and surrounding craft satellites built by iron-using African rice farmers, herders, and fishers.

points.label: Jenné (Museum Trench)
points.description: Eight metres of stratified mud-brick town walls showing demographic overlap and shift from Jenné-jeno into Islamic Jenné.

points.label: Dia (Shoma & Mara mounds)
points.description: Western delta mound complex uniting early Tichitt-heritage rice farming with medieval burial and trade phases.

points.label: Ounjougou (Bandiagara Plateau)
points.description: Upland eastern margin preserving some of Africa’s oldest ceramics and long environmental sequences.

points.label: Sadia (Dogon Plain)
points.description: Mound complex documenting sorghum, pearl millet, and fonio diversification in the delta’s southeastern hinterland.

sections.heading: An urban landscape without a citadel

paragraphs.text: Beginning in the third century BCE atop dry levees above annual Niger floods, early settlers at Jenné-jeno fished, herded cattle, smelted iron, and cultivated domesticated African rice (Oryza glaberrima). Rather than condensing into one walled palace city, habitation expanded outward into over sixty clustered mounds within a 4-kilometre radius.

Archaeologists Susan and Roderick McIntosh interpreted this clustered morphology—lacking monumental royal palaces, temple pyramids, or elite tombs despite surrounding mud-brick city walls built around 850 CE—as a "heterarchical" city organized among cooperative guilds of smiths, potters, herders, fishers, and farmers.

cells: Early Holocene grass-savanna ceramics and microliths
Tichitt-related ceramics, domesticated African rice, medieval burials
Iron smelting, tauf mud architecture, copper imports, 3.3 m town wall
Cluster peak, terracotta art, transition to Islamic market city

sections.heading: Regional subsistence and the transition to historic Jenné

paragraphs.text: Zooarchaeological and archaeobotanical analyses across Jenné-jeno, Dia, and Sadia reveal deliberate risk-buffering across distinct flooding zones: floodwater African rice was balanced with upland pearl millet, fonio, dry-season grazing, and migratory fish catches.

Recent publication of the 1999 Museum excavations inside modern Jenné demonstrates that urban occupation on the new mound began by the late thirteenth or fourteenth century CE—overlapping directly with Jenné-jeno’s final Phase IV rather than following a sudden abandonment.

guides.title: Great Zimbabwe and the Zimbabwe Plateau
guides.description: Monumental dry-stone granite architecture, gold metallurgy, and regional Southern African states across Mapungubwe, Mapela, Great Zimbabwe, and Khami.
guides.intro: Built from fitted courses of split granite without mortar, Great Zimbabwe was Southern Africa’s largest precolonial urban capital. Rather than an isolated marvel, modern Bayesian radiocarbon work places it inside a polycentric network connecting Limpopo Valley centers, southwestern plateau hills, and Indian Ocean gold trade.
guides.scope: Middle-to-Late Iron Age sequences across the Shashe-Limpopo Basin and Zimbabwe Plateau, c. 900–1700 CE.

map.scope: Southern African plateau and Shashe-Limpopo confluence research localities. Points locate monumental capitals and stratified excavations, not territorial borders.

points.label: Great Zimbabwe
points.description: Hill Complex, Great Enclosure, Valley compounds, and surrounding unwalled dhaka town neighborhoods.

points.label: Mapungubwe Hill & K2
points.description: Shashe-Limpopo basin capital where sacred hilltop kingship, stone terracing, and royal gold burials developed.

points.label: Mapela Hill
points.description: Southwestern plateau terraced hilltop revealing monumental elite architecture roughly contemporaneous with K2–Mapungubwe.

points.label: Mtanye
points.description: Southern Zambezian settlement linking Limpopo and plateau agropastoral social networks.

points.label: Khami
points.description: Western Torwa/Butua stone-terraced capital characterized by decorated retaining walls and Ming/European trade goods.

sections.heading: Re-threading the chronology and urban layout

paragraphs.text: Antiquarian treasure hunting by colonial syndicates in the late nineteenth century destroyed crucial stratigraphy inside Great Zimbabwe’s Great Enclosure. Careful re-examination of archival excavations alongside Bayesian radiocarbon modeling shows stone-walled phases overlapping Mapungubwe and peaking in the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries CE.

Beyond the iconic curved granite walls (P-style and Q-style coursing) and Conical Tower, dense residential compounds of beaten dhaka clay floors surrounded the stone enclosures, where residents smelted iron and gold, spun cotton, kept cattle, and hosted craftsmen alongside royal court complexes.

cells: Transition from valley cattle kraal center to sacred hilltop terrace capital
Early terraced prestige walls challenging single-origin models of Zimbabwe complexity
Monolithic soapstone birds, Conical Tower, gold crucibles, and coastal trade ties
Checkered terraced platforms after Great Zimbabwe’s political decentralization

sections.heading: Cattle, gold and Indian Ocean exchange

paragraphs.text: Archaeological syntheses increasingly move away from simple diffusion models toward multi-centric state formation across southern Zambezia. Local alluvial and reef gold mining, cattle herding, and ivory hunting fueled long-distance exchange reaching Swahili ports such as Kilwa Kisiwani.

guides.title: Aksum, Yeha and the Northern Horn Highlands
guides.description: From Pre-Aksumite temples at Yeha and the Red Sea port of Adulis to Aksum’s monolithic stelae and Lalibela’s medieval rock-hewn churches.
guides.intro: Highland communities in northern Ethiopia and Eritrea domesticated teff and finger millet, erected stone temples by 800 BCE, and forged the Kingdom of Aksum—an international power minting its own coinage and linking the African interior with Rome, Persia, and India.
guides.scope: Archaeological sequences across Tigray, Eritrea, and Lasta highlands from c. 800 BCE to the Gondar era.

map.scope: Northern Ethiopian and Eritrean highlands and Red Sea coast locality anchors.

points.label: Aksum (Bieta Giyorgis & Stelae Field)
points.description: Highland capital preserving Pre-Aksumite Ona roots on Bieta Giyorgis, royal monolithic granite stelae, palaces, and coins.

points.label: Yeha
points.description: Pre-Aksumite monumental ashlar temple and elite complex with indigenous crops and Sabaic inscriptions.

points.label: Beta Samati
points.description: Excavated administrative trade town housing one of sub-Saharan Africa’s earliest dated Christian basilicas.

points.label: Adulis (Zula Bay)
points.description: Principal Aksumite Red Sea port channeling African interior goods and Mediterranean/Indian Ocean trade.

points.label: Lalibela
points.description: Eleven monumental monolithic and rock-cut churches carved from volcanic tuff in medieval Lasta.

points.label: Gondar (Fasil Ghebbi)
points.description: Solomonic stone-palace capital grounded by fortified basalt-and-lime royal enclosures.

sections.heading: From Pre-Aksumite highlands to Aksumite statehood

paragraphs.text: Excavations atop Bieta Giyorgis hill overlooking Aksum reveal continuous settlement back into the late first millennium BCE (Pre-Aksumite and Proto-Aksumite Ona phases), showing that Aksum’s rise grew out of indigenous upland ploughed agriculture, cistern management, and highland trade networks.

As the Aksumite Empire expanded from the first to seventh centuries CE, rulers quarried syenite-granite monoliths carved to resemble multi-story towers over underground royal tombs, while secondary centers like Beta Samati and Red Sea port Adulis integrated Mediterranean glass, Roman amphorae, and South Asian trade.

cells: Pre-Aksumite ashlar masonry, D’MT inscriptions, agricultural continuity
Ona precursors, decorated monolithic stelae, Aksumite coins
4th-c. basilica, Ayla-Aksum amphorae, Indian & Roman maritime links
Post-Aksumite rock-hewn churches at Lasta; later stone palaces at Gondar

sections.heading: Highland agriculture, Christianity and later capitals

paragraphs.text: Paleoenvironmental studies indicate indigenous cultural strategies stabilized Ethiopian cereal agriculture across shifting rainfall regimes before and during Aksumite state growth. After Aksum’s political center moved south in the late first millennium CE, medieval Christian monarchs sculpted Lalibela’s sunken church complexes before Gondar rose as the fixed seventeenth-century stone capital.

guides.title: Kilwa Kisiwani and the Swahili Coral-Stone Towns
guides.description: Maritime urbanism from sixth-century earth-and-thatch ports at Unguja Ukuu to coral-limestone mosques, coin minting, and the palace of Kilwa Kisiwani.
guides.intro: Dotting the East African shoreline and offshore islands from Kenya through southern Tanzania, Swahili port towns linked African interior gold, ivory, timber, and iron networks to monsoon-driven Indian Ocean commerce. Beneath iconic white coral ruins lie centuries of earlier African earth-and-timber towns.
guides.scope: Archaeological sequences across Gedi, Chwaka (Pemba), Unguja Ukuu (Zanzibar), Kilwa Kisiwani, and Songo Mnara, c. 550–1600 CE.

map.scope: Swahili coast islands and coastal townlands from central Kenya to southern Tanzania.

points.label: Kilwa Kisiwani & Songo Mnara
points.description: Southern Swahili island capital famous for the domed Great Mosque, Husuni Kubwa clifftop palace, copper/silver coins, and nearby Songo Mnara.

points.label: Unguja Ukuu (Zanzibar)
points.description: First-millennium trading harbor built in wattle-and-daub architecture mixing Tana ceramics, Gulf imports, and Asian rice.

points.label: Chwaka (Pemba Island)
points.description: Urban neighborhood sequence showing four superimposed Porites coral mosques amidst earthen houses.

points.label: Gedi & Mida Creek (Kenya)
points.description: Walled coastal forest town with palace, pillar tombs, Friday Mosque, and mangrove creek outports.

points.label: Lamu Archipelago / Shanga region
points.description: Northern Swahili island cluster charting the gradual timber-to-coral transformation of coastal mosques.

sections.heading: Indigenous African coastal roots and Porites coral urbanism

paragraphs.text: Earlier colonial scholarship falsely portrayed Swahili towns as foreign Arab colonies. Stratified excavations at Unguja Ukuu, Chwaka, and Kilwa refute that claim: early towns grew directly out of Bantu-speaking coastal Iron Age fishing and farming communities using local Tana Tradition pottery centuries before coral-stone mosques replaced timber-and-daub architecture.

Between the eleventh and fifteenth centuries CE, elite Swahili merchants shaped fresh marine Porites coral and lime mortar into vaulted mosques, multi-story courtyard houses, and clifftop palaces such as Husuni Kubwa at Kilwa Kisiwani, surrounded by dense wattle-and-daub urban quarters.

cells: Wattle-and-daub trade harbor, Siraf pottery, Asian rice & cotton
Four sequential coral mosques surrounded by earthen houses
Inland forest stone town linked to creek anchorages

sections.heading: Hard history, enslaved labor and oceanic disruption

paragraphs.text: Recent urban archaeology at Songo Mnara and Zanzibar examines everyday domestic space alongside material signatures of inequality and enslaved labor that sustained maritime ports. Portuguese warships bombarded Kilwa and constructed Fort Santiago in 1505, disrupting independent Swahili monsoon commerce.

guides.title: Kerma, Napata and Meroë: Cities of Kush
guides.description: Nearly three millennia of Nubian statehood along the Middle Nile—from Kerma’s mud-brick Deffufa and cattle-tumulus kingdom to Napatan pyramids and Meroitic ironworks.
guides.intro: Upstream of Egypt’s First Cataract, the Middle Nile Valley hosted a succession of powerful indigenous African kingdoms grouped historically as Kush. Archaeology across Kerma, the Dongola Reach, Napata, Dangeil, and the Royal City of Meroë reveals monumental mud-brick shrines, royal pyramids, alphabetic Meroitic writing, and massive iron-smelting industries.
guides.scope: Archaeological sequences in northern Sudan from Classic Kerma (2500–1500 BCE) through Napatan (9th–4th c. BCE) and Meroitic Kush (c. 300 BCE–350 CE).

map.scope: Middle Nile cataracts and Shendi/Dongola Reach research centers in northern Sudan.

points.label: Kerma (Deffufa & Eastern Cemetery)
points.description: Early Kushite capital combining the towering mud-brick Western Deffufa temple with royal tumuli ringed by hundreds of cattle bucrania.

points.label: Letti Basin (Southern Kerma)
points.description: Newly discovered provincial Kerman settlement illuminating administrative and pastoral networks south of the Third Cataract.

points.label: Jebel Barkal (Napata)
points.description: Sacred sandstone mesa and Napatan capital behind the 25th Dynasty Kushite kings who ruled both Nubia and Egypt.

points.label: Dangeil (Fifth Cataract Amun City)
points.description: Kushite city featuring a monumental Amun temple and stratified crucible workshops for tin-bronze casting.

points.label: Royal City of Meroë
points.description: Southern capital of Kush renowned for royal pyramids, stone temples, Meroitic inscriptions, and extensive iron-smelting slag mounds.

paragraphs.text: Emerging around 2500 BCE independently of Old Kingdom Egypt, Kerma controlled floodplains and desert gold routes around the Third Cataract. At the heart of its urban core stood the solid mud-brick Western Deffufa, flanked by specialized copper/bronze foundries and granaries while provincial towns such as Letti anchored the southern Dongola Reach.

Kerma’s Eastern Cemetery traces the rise of warrior-archer elites and sacred kingship crowned with colossal earthen tumuli accompanied by hundreds of sacrificed cattle skulls—reflecting pastoral ideologies shared across northeastern Africa.

cells: Western Deffufa mud-brick temple, cattle-bucrania tumuli, tin-bronze
25th Dynasty Kushite revival, royal pyramids, Amun precinct
Meroitic script, Dangeil bronze crucibles, 97-date iron slag chronology

sections.heading: From Napata to Meroitic ironworking and Red Sea connections

paragraphs.text: Following Egypt’s New Kingdom withdrawal, local Nubian communities preserved resilient settlements before Napatan rulers united Kush and Egypt in the eighth century BCE. When the royal center later shifted southward to Meroë, Kushite cities developed an indigenous alphabet, cast tin-bronze at Dangeil, and operated long-lived bloomery iron-smelting workshops fueled sustainably by managed Nile Acacia timber.

guides.title: Mecca, the Hijaz and the Hajj Pilgrimage
guides.description: The sanctuary of the Kaaba in Mecca, Medina’s Hijrah landscape, Red Sea crossing ports in Egypt and Sudan, and inland pilgrimage roads across fifteen centuries.
guides.intro: Set in a dry granite valley roughly seventy kilometers inland from the Red Sea coast, Mecca became the sacred center of Islam and the annual destination of the Hajj pilgrimage. Archaeological survey along Red Sea ports, caravan waystations, and early inscriptions shows how African, Mediterranean, and Asian travelers shaped Hijazi infrastructure.
guides.scope: Hijaz sanctuary urbanism, Medina (Yathrib), Historic Jeddah, Darb Zubaydah, and African–Red Sea crossing corridors c. 570–1900 CE.

map.scope: Hijaz and central Red Sea pilgrim crossing zone. Points mark historic sanctuary towns, Red Sea embarkation ports, and surveyed caravan waystations.

points.label: Mecca (al-Masjid al-Ḥarām & Kaaba)
points.description: Focal sanctuary enclosing the Kaaba and Zamzam well; goal of the annual Hajj and daily qibla orientation worldwide.

points.label: Historic Jeddah (Port of Mecca)
points.description: Coral-rag Red Sea port designated as maritime gateway for sea-borne Hajj pilgrims arriving from Suez, ʿAydhāb, Suakin, and East Africa.

points.label: Medina (Yathrib)
points.description: Northern Hijaz oasis city where the 622 CE Hijrah established the Prophet’s Mosque, early community charter, and major Hadith scholarship.

points.label: ʿAydhāb (African Red Sea Hajj port)
points.description: Medieval Nile-to-Red Sea port where Upper Egyptian, North African, and West African pilgrims crossed to Jeddah for two centuries.

points.label: Al-Rabadhah (Darb Zubaydah)
points.description: Excavated Abbasid caravanserai, cisterns, and mosque station along Empress Zubaydah bint Jaʿfar’s Kufa-to-Mecca pilgrimage highway.

points.label: Al-Ḥijr / Hegra (Syro-Egyptian Hajj station)
points.description: Watered oasis fort and caravan halt along the Syrian and Egyptian overland Hajj corridors descending into the Hijaz.

sections.heading: Sanctuary, revelation and the Kaaba in the Hijaz

paragraphs.text: Before the seventh century CE, seasonal sacred fairs and pilgrimage circuits linked Arabian tribes across Mecca and neighboring shrines. Within Islamic scripture and early community memory, Muhammad’s mission (beginning c. 610 CE in Mecca) and the 622 CE migration (Hijrah) to Medina reoriented the Kaaba exclusively toward monotheistic worship, preserving it as the qibla (prayer direction) and liturgical center for Muslims worldwide.

Archaeological analysis of early Abbasid marble, basalt, and mosaic inscriptions from the Sacred Mosque alongside architectural reconstructions of early Kaaba courtyards demonstrates massive state patronage—caliphs widened the circumambulation colonnades, gilded waterspouts, and institutionalized water supply from the Zamzam well and Ayn Zubaydah aqueducts.

Coral-stone maritime gateway linking African Nile & Swahili fleets to Mecca

sections.heading: African, Asian and Red Sea pilgrimage highways

paragraphs.text: Making the Hajj transformed cities across Africa into intellectual and logistical nodes. Caravans from Walata, Timbuktu, Kano, and Bornu marched north via Cairo or Lake Chad–Darfur toward Egypt and Sudan, sailing across the Red Sea from ʿAydhāb or Suakin into Historic Jeddah before ascending the coastal escarpment toward Mecca.

guides.title: Islam: origins, branches, law schools and global networks
guides.description: An introduction to Sunni, Shīʿī (Twelver, Ismāʿīlī, Zaydī), Ibāḍī, legal madhhabs, and Sufi traditions linking Arabia, Africa, the Mediterranean, and Asia.
guides.intro: Shared commitment to the Qur’an, Muhammad’s prophetic example, prayer, alms, Ramadan fasting, and Hajj toward Mecca unites Muslim communities globally—yet historical debates over early leadership, legal interpretation, theology, and spiritual guidance produced distinct Sunni, Shīʿī, Ibāḍī, and Sufi traditions.
guides.scope: Comparative historical geography of early Islamic communities, succession debates, legal schools (madhhabs), Imamate lineages, Ibāḍī oases, and Sufi networks c. 610–1900 CE.

map.scope: Representative historic centers of Sunni, Shīʿī, Ibāḍī, and Sufi scholarship across Africa, the Middle East, and western Indian Ocean rims.

points.label: Mecca & Medina
points.description: Sacred cradle of the Qur’an, earliest Muslim community charter at Yathrib (Medina), and shared Hajj sanctuary across branches.

points.label: Kufa, Karbala & Baghdad
points.description: Formative Iraqi cradle of Imāmī (Twelver) Shīʿī shrines and theology alongside classical Ḥanafī, Ḥanbalī, and early Sufi circles.

points.label: Fusṭāṭ & Historic Cairo (Al-Azhar)
points.description: Founded under North African Fāṭimid Ismāʿīlī Shīʿī rule (969 CE) before Ayyubid and Mamluk patronage turned al-Azhar into a premier Sunni institution.

points.label: Kairouan (Great Mosque & Mālikī Center)
points.description: North African foundation city whose scholars helped codify the Sunni Mālikī legal school across the Maghreb and West Africa.

points.label: Tahert & M’zab Valley (Ibāḍī centers)
points.description: Heartlands of North African Ibāḍī governance—first at eighth-century Rustamid Tahert and enduringly in the fortified oasis pentapolis of the M’zab.

points.label: Timbuktu & Inland Niger Delta
points.description: West African hub of Mālikī jurisprudence, manuscript libraries, and Sufi scholarly brotherhoods spanning Qādiriyyah and Tijāniyyah lineages.

points.label: Kilwa & Zanzibar (Swahili Coast)
points.description: Coastal towns predominantly following Sunni Shāfiʿī jurisprudence later joined by Omani Ibāḍī rulers in Zanzibar and South Asian Ismāʿīlī communities.

points.label: Nizwa & Coastal Oman
points.description: Historic seat of the Ibāḍī Imamate and maritime networks linking Arabian Sea trade with Swahili Zanzibar and East Africa.

sections.heading: Succession after 632 CE: Sunni, Shīʿī, and Ibāḍī branches

paragraphs.text: Following the death of Muhammad in 632 CE, Muslims divided over who rightly held spiritual and political authority over the ummah (community). Historians emphasize that mature doctrinal identities crystalized gradually across the seventh to tenth centuries rather than springing fully formed at a single moment.

Sunni Muslims (Ahl al-Sunnah wa-l-Jamāʿah, historically 85–90% of Muslims) affirmed the consensus community leadership of the first four Rightly Guided Caliphs and transmitted Prophetic practice through canonical Hadith and legal jurisprudence. Shīʿī Muslims (Shīʿat ʿAlī) held that inspired leadership belonged by designation to the Prophet’s cousin and son-in-law ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib and an inherited line of Imāms from the Prophet’s household (Ahl al-Bayt), branching into Twelver (Ithnā ʿAsharī), Ismāʿīlī (who established the North African Fāṭimid Caliphate and founded Cairo in 969 CE), and Zaydī traditions.

A third major surviving branch, Ibāḍī Islam, emerged from seventh-century Basran piety movements that rejected both dynastic Umayyad/Abbasid claims and the militant exclusionism of armed Khārijī factions, teaching that the Imāmate belongs to the most pious qualified scholar chosen by consensus regardless of ancestry. Ibāḍī states flourished across interior Oman (Nizwa) and North Africa (Rustamid Tahert, Algeria’s M’zab Valley, Jebel Nafusa, and Djerba), later shaping nineteenth-century East Africa around Zanzibar alongside Shāfiʿī and Ismāʿīlī neighbors.

Ḥanafī (Turkey, Central/South Asia), Mālikī (Maghreb, West Africa via Kairouan/Timbuktu), Shāfiʿī (East Africa/Swahili, Egypt, SE Asia), Ḥanbalī (Arabia)

sections.heading: Schools of law, Sufism and African-Asian syntheses

paragraphs.text: Within Sunni Islam, four classical schools of jurisprudence (*madhhabs*) crystallized around Iraq and Medina by the ninth century CE: Ḥanafī, Mālikī, Shāfiʿī, and Ḥanbalī, mutually recognizing one another as valid interpretive paths rather than rival sects. Across Africa, Islamic learning traveled primarily along merchant caravans and scholar-pilgrim networks—Mālikī manuals copied in Kairouan, Fez, and Timbuktu shaped Saharan courts, while Shāfiʿī scholarship along Red Sea and monsoon lanes connected Aden, Kilwa, and Malabar, and Sufi teaching orders deepened vernacular devotion.

guides.title: Christianity: early churches, councils, branches and global traditions
guides.description: How Christological councils, imperial politics, monasticisms, African kingdoms, and European Reformations shaped the Church of the East, Oriental Orthodox, Eastern Orthodox, Catholic, Protestant, and independent traditions.
guides.intro: Christian communities emerged across West Asia, North and Northeast Africa, and the Mediterranean long before Europe became predominantly Christian. Over two millennia, theological debates over the nature of Christ, church governance, liturgy, and scripture produced distinct ecclesiastical families across continents.
guides.scope: Institutional, archaeological, and liturgical history across the Church of the East, Oriental Orthodox (Coptic, Ethiopian, Nubian, Syriac, Armenian), Eastern Orthodox, Roman Catholic, and Protestant/Independent traditions through 1900 CE.

map.scope: Key patriarchal, archaeological, and Reformation centers shaping Christian diversity across Africa, West Asia, and Europe.

points.label: Jerusalem & Antioch
points.description: Earliest Jewish-Christian and Gentile-mission centers in Judea and Roman Syria, shaping early liturgy and scriptural canon.

points.label: Seleucia-Ctesiphon / Baghdad (Church of the East)
points.description: Patriarchal heartland of the East Syriac Church of the East outside Roman borders, sending missions to South India and Tang China.

points.label: Alexandria & Abu Mena (Coptic Orthodox)
points.description: Ancient catechetical and patriarchal seat of the Coptic Orthodox Church, birthplace of Christian desert monasticism and non-Chalcedonian Miaphysite theology.

points.label: Old Dongola (Makurian Nubia)
points.description: Capital of Christian Nubia (Makuria, with Nobatia and Alwa) preserving cathedral murals, bilingual Greek-Coptic-Old Nubian manuscripts, and monasteries.

points.label: Aksum & Lalibela (Ethiopian Tewahedo)
points.description: Fourth-century Aksumite royal adoption of Christianity, early Beta Samati basilica, Ge’ez scriptural canon, and Lalibela rock-hewn churches.

points.label: Carthage & Hippo Regius (North Africa)
points.description: Cradle of Latin Christian theology (Tertullian, Cyprian, Augustine) and centuries of Catholic–Donatist church controversy in Roman Africa.

points.label: Constantinople (Eastern Orthodox)
points.description: Eastern Roman capital hosting major ecumenical councils (381–787 CE) and focal seat of Chalcedonian Eastern Orthodoxy.

points.label: Rome (Roman Catholic)
points.description: Patriarchal seat of Latin-rite Roman Catholicism spanning medieval Western Christendom, Trent, and global missionary expansion.

points.label: Wittenberg & Northern Europe (Reformations)
points.description: Sixteenth-century epicenters of Lutheran, Reformed/Calvinist, Anglican, and Anabaptist/Radical branches emphasizing vernacular scripture.

points.label: Mbanza Kongo (Kingdom of Kongo Catholicism)
points.description: Sovereign African Catholic kingdom under Nzinga a Nkuwu and Afonso I blending Kongo political cosmology, stone churches, and Kikongo literacy.

sections.heading: Conciliar divisions (431 & 451 CE) and the ancient Eastern churches

paragraphs.text: Long before Western Europe fragmented in the sixteenth century, ancient debates over how divinity and humanity unite in Jesus Christ divided Christianity along linguistic and imperial frontiers. At the Council of Ephesus (431 CE), Syriac-speaking churches in Sasanian Persia upheld a two-nature distinction (Dyophysitism) associated with Theodore of Mopsuestia, developing as the independent Church of the East (historically mislabeled "Nestorian") stretching across Baghdad to India and China.

Twenty years later, the Council of Chalcedon (451 CE) defined Christ as one person in two distinct natures—precipitating a permanent rupture. Pro-Chalcedonian imperial churches anchored Eastern Orthodoxy (Greek/Slavic Byzantine communion, formally estranged from Latin Rome in 1054) and Roman Catholicism, while non-Chalcedonian Oriental Orthodox churches (Coptic Egypt, Ethiopian and Eritrean Tewahedo, Syriac, Armenian, and Indian Malankara) preserved Cyril of Alexandria’s formula of one united incarnate divine-human nature (Miaphysitism, often inaccurately called "Monophysitism").

Iconographic liturgy, Hesychasm, married parish clergy, autocephalous patriarchates (Constantinople, Russia, Greece, Balkans)

sections.heading: Roman Catholicism, Reformations, and African Christian appropriations

paragraphs.text: Beginning in 1517 CE, European Reformations fractured Western Latin Catholicism into Lutheran, Reformed/Calvinist, Anglican (retaining historic episcopacy), and Radical/Anabaptist traditions, followed in subsequent centuries by Wesleyan/Methodist, Baptist, restorationist, and nineteenth-century holiness movements.

Across Africa, Christianity is neither solely European nor solely modern: Alexandria and Carthage produced foundational church fathers and desert monasticism, Aksum’s fourth-century kings and medieval Lalibela and Nubian Dongola sustained vibrant indigenous churches for over a millennium, King Afonso I built an African Catholic kingdom in Kongo from 1506 onward, and nineteenth-century converts pioneered independent African churches interpreting translated scriptures on local terms.

guides.title: Trade on the Mediterranean Sea: ports, shipwrecks and connected civilizations
guides.description: How five millennia of maritime shipping—from Byblos timber ships and the Uluburun wreck to Phoenician-Greek colonies, Roman Portus, Cairo Geniza networks, and Suez—tied Africa, West Asia, and Europe together.
guides.intro: Far from dividing Africa, West Asia, and Europe, the enclosed Mediterranean Sea served for five thousand years as the world’s cheapest heavy-freight highway. Carrying grain, copper ingots, olive oil, timber, glass, silk, enslaved people, and scripts from port to port, merchant hulls transformed shore towns across all three continents.
guides.scope: Archaeology of Bronze Age shipwrecks, Phoenician and Greek colonies, Hellenistic/Roman concrete harbors, and medieval–modern shipping networks across the Mediterranean, c. 3000 BCE–1900 CE.

map.scope: Selected archaeological harbors and sealed shipwrecks connecting African, West Asian, and European shorelines.

points.description: Atlantic gateway linking Tartessian silver, tin, and Baetican olive oil into Mediterranean shipping.

points.label: Massalia (Marseille)
points.description: Phocaean port at the Rhône estuary linking inland Gaul with Greek wine and coin.

points.label: Carthage & Al-Mahdiyya corridor
points.description: Central Tunisian sea-crossing linking Maghrebi wheat, purple textiles, Saharan gold, and Geniza fleets.

points.label: Ostia & Imperial Portus
points.description: Claudian–Trajanic megaharbor receiving Egyptian and North African annona grain convoys.

points.label: Venice & Adriatic Lagoon
points.description: Assembly-line Arsenale and state galley mudae connecting northern Europe with Alexandria and Syria.

points.label: Syracuse
points.description: Twin-harbor Sicilian bottleneck bridging Aegean, Italic, and North African shipping lanes.

points.label: Delos & Corinth Corridor
points.description: Cycladic Roman free port and Aegean commercial hub tied to Corinthian portage and stamped amphorae.

points.label: Alexandria (Pharos Harbor)
points.description: Monumental twin-harbor metropolis funneling Nile grain and Red Sea monsoon spices to the Mediterranean.

points.label: Constantinople (Yenikapı)
points.description: Theodosian Harbor preserving 37 excavated Byzantine cargo vessels across Mediterranean–Black Sea straits.

points.label: Byblos, Tyre & Ugarit (Levantine Coast)
points.description: Ancient Lebanese–Syrian timber, purple dye, alphabet, and glassmaking mother-ports.

sections.heading: Bronze Age hulls to Phoenician and Greek container networks

paragraphs.text: Maritime logistics enabled metallurgy and urbanization long before iron tools. Third-millennium Byblos cedar convoys supplied treeless Egypt’s temples and royal hulls, while the fourteenth-century BCE Uluburun shipwreck off southwest Turkey reveals ten tons of Cypriot copper paired with Central Asian tin, Syrian resin, raw cobalt glass ingots, and African ivory—all carried in a single mortise-and-tenon hull.

Following the Late Bronze crisis, Phoenician merchants from Tyre and Sidon and Aegean sailors from Corinth, Euboea, and Ionia knit the entire basin together from Nile Naukratis to Carthage, Syracuse, Massalia, and Atlantic Cádiz. Standardized clay transport amphorae ("containerization"), silver coinage, and the West Semitic–Greek alphabets spread swiftly along these commercial shipping lanes.

cells: Byblos timber ships, Minoan Kommos, Ugarit archives, Uluburun shipwreck (copper/tin/glass/ivory)
Tyre, Carthage, Gadir/Cádiz, Corinth Diolkos, Massalia, Naukratis; alphabet & coined silver spread

sections.heading: Hydraulic concrete empires, Yenikapı hulls and the Geniza merchants

paragraphs.text: Integrating Campanian volcanic-ash hydraulic concrete allowed Roman engineers at Caesarea Maritima and Imperial Portus to pour massive artificial harbors directly into open seas, supporting grain fleets (annona) of up to 1,200 tons per ship alongside Baetican and African oil cargoes stacked sky-high in Rome’s Monte Testaccio.

Maritime exchange remained polycentric rather than halting with western Rome: Constantinople’s 37 Yenikapı hulls trace structural frame-first shipbuilding evolution; the 1025 CE Serçe Limanı vessel carried three tons of Islamic Syrian glass cullet for Byzantine recyclers; Cairo Geniza letters chronicle dense eleventh-century Muslim–Jewish business agency between Egypt, Tunisia, and Sicily; and Amalfi, Pisa, Genoa, and Venice institutionalized marine insurance, partnerships, and convoy shipping before the 1869 Suez Canal united Mediterranean waters directly with Indian Ocean steamships.
